citation: Unattributed drawing of a log building on a shore, with a woman in its doorway, a crowd of children on the bank, canoes afloat and drawn up, and a white lighthouse tower on a low point in the middle distance. Deposited by the repository owner on 2026-09-03 with the description "a great pic of the shore along there and the eliza chappel school at clark and lake". Taken from a 2018 Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal post on Chappell (drloih_chappell), where it is the first image, uncredited: a republication.
describes_date: not established, and the lighthouse does not establish it. T-0649 read the tower and it carries the 1832 tower's signature (tapered shaft, railed gallery, domed lantern, finial) and nothing sharper: on a 12 px shaft the gallery overhang is 1.25 against the 1838 plate's 1.208, and +/-1 px is +/-0.08, so the agreement distinguishes the Chicago harbour light from no other conical harbour light of the period. A tower of that kind is therefore drawn and nothing more; it is not a terminus post quem this record may rest on.
repository: THE IMMEDIATE SOURCE IS NOW KNOWN, BUT THE ORIGINAL IS NOT (T-0909, 2026-10-09). The owner named it on 2026-09-24: the deposited file came from the Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal post of 19 January 2018 (drloih_chappell). An archived copy of the post (Wayback, 2026-06-06) confirms it: the post's first image is 21617595_10203558686525015_5452300313452439832_n.jpg, the same social-media filename the deposit carries. It is captioned only "The Eliza Chappell School was roughly at Lake and Clark Streets are today." and has no artist, date, publication or holding institution, and the journal says it "does not use inline citations on purpose". So the post is one link in the chain, a republication, and the drawing's own repository is still unestablished. Before that: T-0663 (2026-09-04) eliminated Andreas 1884, the Porter memoir 1892, Kirkland 1892 and Quaife's Checagou 1933, each by reading its list of illustrations, and T-0716 (2026-09-06) showed that the one candidate left, William Mark Young's 'Chicago's First School House' of about 1925 for Koopman, Robinson & Neumer, is a different picture: the 1844 Rumsey School, by its own inscribed caption. docs/RESEARCH/chappel_shore_origin_search.md is the full record.
rights_note: Republished without credit, which clears nothing (T-0909). The 2018 journal post the file was taken from credits no artist and states no terms, and a blog's reuse of a picture is not a licence to reuse it here, so under AGENTS.md rule 6 this drawing is cited in text and no asset is derived from it. Provenance of the original is unknown. Provenance unknown. Until the original is located with its terms stated, cite in text and derive no asset from it. It arrives without artist, date or repository, so it cannot yet be argued out of copyright on age the way the Braunhold and Trowbridge plates can - AND THE SHARPER VERSION OF THAT WORRY IS NOW DEAD. T-0663 raised it: the one live candidate was a commercial print of about 1925, and if it proved to be the source then age stopped being an argument at all and this became a live rights question. T-0716 compared the pictures and the candidate is not the source, so that particular alarm is withdrawn. What remains is the plain unknown it always was: no artist, no date, no terms, so rights_status stays check_required and nothing is derived from it.
note:
THE OWNER NAMED THE IMMEDIATE SOURCE, AND IT DOES NOT SETTLE THE ORIGIN (T-0909, 2026-10-09). The deposit came from the Digital Research Library of Illinois History Journal's 2018 post on Eliza Chappell, already committed as drloih_chappell for its account of the school. The drawing is that post's first image, uncredited. That answers route 2 of docs/RESEARCH/chappel_shore_origin_search.md § 6, ask the depositor, and it moves nothing else: describes_date, tier 5, verified false and rights_status check_required all stand, because a republication is not the original. It also explains the caption. The deposit's "eliza chappel school at clark and lake" follows the post's caption, which gives the school's 1834 corner, so the disagreement between caption and picture noted below is between a 2018 compiler and the drawing, not within the drawing. The artist and original-publication search is not reopened unless a lead turns up.

FILED BEFORE IT IS SPENT, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THIS RECORD (T-0617, 2026-09-04), STILL NOT SPENT AFTER T-0649 READ ITS LIGHTHOUSE (2026-09-04), STILL NOT SPENT AFTER T-0663 WENT LOOKING FOR ITS ORIGINAL (2026-09-04), AND STILL NOT SPENT AFTER T-0716 KILLED THE ONE CANDIDATE THAT SEARCH LEFT STANDING (2026-09-06).

THE EXTERNAL ROUTE WAS RUN AND IT DID NOT FIND THE ORIGINAL. docs/RESEARCH/chappel_shore_origin_search.md is the record, written so the next run does not re-ask the same questions. What it closes: Andreas's History of Chicago vol. I (1884) lists exactly one Chappel plate, the portrait at p. 206, and nothing captioned school-house, shore, canoe or lighthouse; the Porter memoir of 1892 carries no list of illustrations at all; Kirkland's Story of Chicago (1892) lists none of those subjects either; and the digitised Checagou (1933) has neither a plate list nor the name Chappel.

AND THE FIFTH ANSWER IS NOW CLOSED TOO, ON THE PICTURE RATHER THAN ON THE TITLE (T-0716). T-0663 left one candidate alive on two secondary-market listing titles - William Mark Young, 'Chicago's First School House', ca. 1925, for Koopman, Robinson & Neumer - and could not reach the pictures, so nothing in this project was allowed to name him. The pictures were reached: two impressions of the one plate, at 1599 px and at 721 x 1024. IT IS NOT THIS SHEET, and it fails all four tests at once. The building at the right is a TWO-STOREY CLAPBOARD frame with a stoop and six windows on the near face, not a one-storey saddle-notched log house. NOBODY STANDS IN ITS DOORWAY; the schoolmistress is out in the street in 1840s crinoline. THERE IS NO WATER IN IT - no shore, no conical light on a point, and so nothing to crop a lighthouse out of. AND THERE ARE NO CANOES. The plate then answers the question itself: along its bottom margin, in the artist's hand, 'Chicago's first school house, erected 1844, called "The Rumsey School". Located on the southeast corner of Madison and Dearborn streets.', signed Wm Mark Young and marked Co. Koopman-Robinson-Neumer. That is the 1844 Rumsey school at Madison and Dearborn - the other building the phrase names, and the exact confusion the test was set up to catch. Medium and format part them as well: Young's plate is a portrait ETCHING built wholly from hatched line, and this sheet is a landscape continuous-tone drawing, 640 x 368, reproduced as a halftone.

WHAT THAT LEAVES. No candidate at all, which is a cleaner state than a candidate nobody had looked at. The rest of Young's 1925 campaign for the same studio - Chicago's First Stage Depot, La Salle Street 1889, Chicago Gateway, a Chicago River view - has NOT been examined; it is written down in the research file as a last-resort lead, resting on nothing but the same hand having drawn old Chicago, and the etched-line argument above tells against the whole campaign rather than the one plate. The cheapest question on the list is still unasked and is now the first one: WHERE DID THE DEPOSITOR GET THE SCAN.

WHAT IT SHOWS. A one-storey LOG building at the right, gable roof, a door and two windows on the near face, saddle-notched corners; a woman in a white apron standing in the doorway; girls in bonnets and aprons streaming along the bank toward it. To the left, a shore: one canoe afloat with paddlers, two more drawn up with figures around them. In the middle distance a white lighthouse tower on a low point, and beyond it a scatter of small gabled buildings on a flat prairie horizon.

THE CAPTION AND THE PICTURE DISAGREE, AND THAT IS STILL THE USEFUL PART. Clark and Lake is inland, and the 1834 destination of Chappell's school on that corner was the FRAME First Presbyterian Church - not a log building, and not on a shore. Two readings are open and this record asserts neither:
  (a) It is Chappell's FIRST school of September 1833, the "small log house formerly used as a store" that the Beaubien material identifies as Mark Beaubien's own original cabin beside the Sauganash at Lake and Market. On this reading the picture is a FIFTH view of the Sauganash's log annex, and the most informative one, because it shows the building nearly square-on.
  (b) It is some other log schoolhouse, in which case it belongs to whatever record it does depict and not to the Sauganash at all.

T-0649 SETTLED THE FORK BY REFUSING IT, AND PRINTED THE NUMBERS THAT REFUSE IT. tools/measure_chappel_shore_lighthouse.py, banked in tools/chappel_shore_lighthouse_baseline.json and re-checked by tools/check.sh, measured the sheet against docs/RESEARCH/chappel_shore_lighthouse.md's acceptance:
  * THE PICTURE IS NOT A CONSTRUCTION. Three adults standing on the same bank at depressions of 80, 140 and 144 px below the fitted horizon (y=215, straight to 2.47 px over 63 prairie columns) are drawn 55, 61 and 65 px tall. One station demands that the nearest be drawn 1.80x the furthest; it is drawn 1.18x - short by 1.523x - and the three ratios r = drawn/depression, which must be identical, spread by 1.578x. No drawn position on this sheet can be inverted to a station, and the error is larger than the difference between the stations on offer.
  * THE TOWER'S FOOT IS NOT DRAWN. The lit shaft ends at y=221, the two buildings standing on the tower's own ground have feet at y=233, and the water's edge crosses its column at y=249. Depression is the denominator of every metric inversion and it runs 6 to 34 px, so the drawn tower is between 4.65 and 23.41 m - 15 to 77 feet. Andreas's forty feet is inside that band and so is nearly everything else.
  * FORT DEARBORN IS NOT DRAWN BESIDE THE LIGHT, and this one needs no horizon and no focal length, because two things at the same distance are drawn in the ratio of their real sizes. The committed palisade is 53.0 m square and stands 35.1 m from the light, so beside a 48 px tower it would be 209 px wide - a third of the sheet. The widest unbroken mass actually flanking the tower is 7 px, 3.4 % of a palisade. Either the artist omitted the fort, or the tower is not the Chicago harbour light; either way the tower stops being usable as a control.
  * WHAT THE SAUGANASH CORNER WOULD REQUIRE, taken at its most favourable: the corner is 1066.3 m from the light on the committed coordinates, bearing 70.3 deg, which is the right composition. It needs a focal length of 4,919 to 7,762 px on a 640 px sheet - a horizontal field of 4.7 to 7.4 degrees - and puts the nearest drawn adult 133 to 240 m from the artist.
  * THE ONE POSITIVE. The log building IS drawn square-on: its doorcase head is horizontal to a slope of -0.0102 over a 33 px run, residual 0.358 px. That is what makes the picture tempting and it buys nothing metric, because the sheet is not a construction.

WHAT MAY NOT BE DONE WITH IT. Unchanged, and now measured rather than assumed. It is an undated retrospective drawing by an unnamed hand, COMPOSED RATHER THAN CONSTRUCTED. It may not move an attributed plate - Braunhold, Petford, Trowbridge - on any axis where the two disagree. Where it agrees with them it corroborates; where it is alone it is a single weak view, graded the way T-0092 graded the shutter leaves. It may not be spent as a fifth view of the Sauganash's log annex.

access_notes: The 2018 post is behind a captcha for this runner (2026-10-09), but the Wayback Machine serves it: the snapshot of 2026-06-06 at archived_url carries the post's text and both of its images, and the image's blogger.googleusercontent.com address ends in the deposited filename. The sheet cannot identify itself. Measured on the deposited file: no white margin on any edge and a dark bleed at the bottom, so any printed caption was cropped away before it reached us; the signature smear at the lower left is about 20 x 20 px and resolves into nothing legible at twelvefold enlargement under autocontrast. Identification therefore has to come from a catalogue, and docs/RESEARCH/chappel_shore_origin_search.md section 4 lists which routes are BLOCKED from the automation runner and which are merely negative - the difference is stated per route. ONE OF THOSE WALLS CAME DOWN IN T-0716 and the method is written down there: eBay item pages still 403, but PicClick's SEARCH page does not, it yields eBay's own image id, and i.ebayimg.com serves the full-resolution file unblocked. That is what put Young's plate in front of a reader. Still shut: HathiTrust full-text search, WorthPoint, Explore Chicago Collections, images.chicagohistory.org, the Google Books API on this shared IP. Clean negatives rather than walls: the Art Institute API and the Smithsonian Open Access API both hold no William Mark Young at all.
